questions.question: Which parts of the ear are set into vibration when a sound wave enters?
options: The outer ear canal and the auditory nerve
The eardrum, the tiny bones inside the ear, and the cochlea
Only the brainstem and outer cartilage
The nerve endings in the skin of the outer ear

questions.question: How are sound vibrations converted into electrical signals that travel to the brain?
options: The eardrum acts as an electrical generator sending current directly to the brain.
The tiny bones in the middle ear produce magnetic pulses.
Specialised cells in the cochlea sense the vibrations and send signals along a nerve.
Air pressure changes bypass the nerves and go straight to the brain.

questions.question: What is the typical frequency range detected by human ears, and which frequencies are they most sensitive to?
options: 10 Hz to 10 kHz, being most sensitive to 1–2 kHz
20 Hz to 20 kHz, being most sensitive to 2–5 kHz
50 Hz to 50 kHz, being most sensitive to 5–10 kHz
2 Hz to 200 Hz, being most sensitive to 20–50 Hz

questions.question: What names are given to sound waves with frequencies below 20 Hz and above 20 kHz, respectively?
options: Ultrasound and infrasound
Subsonic and supersonic
Micro-waves and macro-waves
Infrasound and ultrasound

questions.question: As a sound wave travels through the air, how do individual air particles move?
options: Each bit of air vibrates parallel to the wave travel direction without moving permanently forward.
The air particles are pushed all the way from the sound source to the listener's ear.
Each bit of air vibrates perpendicular to the direction of the wave travel.
The air particles spin in tiny circles and drift slowly backwards.

questions.question: Why is sound classified as a longitudinal wave?
options: The direction of vibration is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
The direction of vibration is parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
The wave can only travel over extremely long distances.
The particles of the medium do not vibrate at all.

questions.question: Why does sound travel faster in solids and liquids compared to gases?
options: Liquids and solids contain special magnetic fields that speed up sound.
The particles in gases are too heavy to vibrate.
Solids and liquids are always much hotter than gases.
The particles are very close together, making it easy to pass on vibrations.

questions.question: Why do sound waves travel even faster in solids than in liquids?
options: Solids have larger gaps between their particles than liquids.
Liquids have much stronger chemical bonds than solids.
The strong forces between particles in solids mean vibrations travel even faster.
Solids are transparent to sound waves, which prevents absorption.

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding the speed of sound in air compared to other states of matter?
options: It is about 340 m/s in air, faster in liquids, and faster still in solids.
It is about 1500 m/s in air, slower in liquids, and slowest in solids.
It is about 300,000,000 m/s in air and does not change in liquids or solids.
It is about 340 m/s in air, slower in liquids, and fastest in solids.

questions.question: What occurs when a sound wave reflects from a hard surface, travels back, and is heard again?
options: Refraction
An echo
Dispersion
Absorption

questions.question: Which equation is used to calculate the speed or distance of sound waves?
options: speed = distance × time
speed = time ÷ distance
speed = distance ÷ time
speed = distance + time

questions.question: In an experiment measuring the speed of sound, what is the benefit of using longer distances and longer times?
options: It guarantees that the speed of sound will increase during the experiment.
It reduces the humidity of the air so that sound travels faster.
It completely eliminates the need to use a stopwatch or timing device.
Any measurement errors make up a smaller proportion of the measurements.

questions.question: How is ultrasound used to image structures inside the human body?
options: It reflects from the boundaries between different types of tissues.
It burns away outer tissues so that inner tissues can be photographed.
It uses high-energy radiation to dye the bones a different color.
It causes the organs to emit visible light that is captured by a camera.

questions.question: Why are water waves described as transverse waves?
options: The direction of oscillation is parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
They can only travel through solid barriers.
The direction of oscillation is 90° to the direction of energy transfer.
They do not transfer any energy as they move.

questions.question: What does the amplitude of a water wave represent?
options: The total distance from the start of the wave to its very end.
The greatest distance water moves above and below the rest position.
The number of complete wave cycles that pass a point each second.
The speed at which the wave crest travels across the water's surface.
